title: Pune Dengue Surge Crosses 3,154 Suspected Cases as Child's Suspected Death Draws Scrutiny
excerpt: PMC counts 2 confirmed dengue deaths and 5 under audit, hospitals report bed shortages and 1-2 day admission waits, and corporators demand a full report on mosquito control.
body:
• Pune has recorded 3,154 suspected dengue cases this year (2,413 from within city limits), with 553 in October alone; officials count 2 confirmed dengue deaths and 5 more deaths under audit, including a young girl reported as age 8 by Indian Express/DCN and age 9 by Hindustan Times/Free Press Journal.
  • Act on absolute steps at home: empty, scrub and dry coolers, drums and plant trays once every 7 days — Aedes mosquitoes can breed in as little as 50 ml of standing water and bite in daylight, peaking morning and late afternoon.
  • Watch days 3-7, when fever falls: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, lethargy or rapid breathing mean go to hospital immediately — the fever drop is the danger window, not recovery.
  • Do not take ibuprofen, aspirin or naproxen if dengue is suspected — they raise bleeding risk; paracetamol under medical supervision is the standard fever medicine in the guidance reviewed.

Pune's dengue surge has turned political and clinical at the same time. The Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) told its Standing Committee the city has logged 3,154 suspected dengue cases, of which 2,413 were patients from within Pune and the rest from outside city limits, according to DCN News. October contributed 553 suspected cases, after 726 in September and 568 in August. The same briefing listed 2 confirmed dengue-related deaths and 5 deaths under audit.

The death that focused the meeting was a young girl's. Corporator Nisha Manavatkar raised the death of an eight-year-old girl who had been in hospital; officials said the child had underlying health conditions. The Indian Express headline likewise described an 8-year-old in what it called the city's first suspected dengue death this year, while Hindustan Times and the Free Press Journal described a 9-year-old who died within 48 hours of hospitalisation. The Videshi is reporting the age as 8-9 because the publications disagree, and the death remains 'suspected' until the audit confirms the cause. An elderly woman from Gokhalenagar also died after contracting dengue, the committee was told.

How the surge built

The earlier PMC snapshot, reported on October 18 by DCN News and Health and Family, counted 2,009 suspected cases from January to mid-October — 484 in August, 508 in September and 346 in the first half of October — with 97 confirmed cases and 35 chikungunya cases in Mirror Now's tally. Civic teams found 2,651 mosquito-breeding sites across homes, offices, schools and housing societies by October 14, collected about Rs 5.7 lakh in administrative charges, and said they had inspected more than 13 lakh properties. Kothrud, Aundh-Baner and Nagar Road-Wadgaon Sheri each reported more than 200 suspected cases.

"I was left wondering whether the municipal corporation's health department itself had contracted dengue. Officials were unable to answer any questions about the disease, so a comprehensive report has been sought from them."

— Shrinath Bhimale, Standing Committee Chairman, PMC

Impact: hospitals full, control staff questioned

Hospitals are feeling the caseload. Mirror Now reported a critical shortage of beds, elective surgeries deferred, and waits of one to two days for admission, with dengue and typhoid together driving demand. Hospitals are triaging patients with falling platelet counts, comorbidities or warning signs first, and advising milder cases to recover at home with hydration and rest. Standard cases resolve in three to four days; complicated cases can stay more than a week.

Corporators questioned what 265 mosquito-control employees were doing, and said officials blamed an expired insecticide-spraying contract and staff shortage for delays. Additional Municipal Commissioner Pavneet Kaur ordered ward offices to intensify prevention and to collect patient data from government and private hospitals, clinics and other facilities. Health department head Nina Borade said cases typically rise after the monsoon in August, September and October. A two-and-a-half-year-old from Vaibhav Colony in Tingrenagar spent eight days in intensive care at Sassoon General Hospital before going home; her family said no spraying had been done at their home, where three members were infected.

What's next

The Standing Committee has demanded a comprehensive report covering infected patients, affected areas, hospital admissions and breeding sites, and corporators want breeding-site elimination, stagnant-water drainage at construction sites and door-to-door awareness without delay. For families in Pune — and diaspora readers with parents and children there — the next week matters at household level: run the 7-day dry-day check, cover stored water forced by supply cuts, and treat any fever that improves then produces abdominal pain, vomiting or bleeding as an emergency, not a recovery.
